details:
**Francis Fukuyama, The End of History and the Last Man**
Fukuyama's 1992 book, which grew out of a 1989 essay, argued that the triumph of liberal democracy after the Cold War marked the "end of history," meaning the endpoint of humanity's ideological evolution. The "last man" in the title is borrowed from Nietzsche.

**Thomas Carlyle's "Great Man" theory**
Carlyle argued, notably in On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), that history is largely shaped by the deeds of heroic individuals. Social historians oppose this view by stressing the role of ordinary people and broad social forces.

**Hegel's Lectures on the Philosophy of History**
G.W.F. Hegel saw history as the self-unfolding of the World Spirit (Weltgeist) and as progress in the consciousness of freedom. In the Oriental world "one is free," in the Greek and Roman world "some are free," and in the Germanic world "all are free." He notoriously claimed that Africa was "no historical part of the world." Hegel also wrote that the "owl of Minerva" spreads its wings only at dusk, meaning that philosophy understands an era only after it has passed.

**Herodotus, "the Father of History"**
The Greek author of the Histories, an account of the Greco-Persian Wars, whom Cicero called the father of history. Other famous historians mentioned in clues include Thucydides, Livy, Edward Gibbon (The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire), David McCullough, and Stephen Ambrose.

**Giambattista Vico, The New Science**
Vico's 1725 work presents a cyclical theory of history. Nations pass through an age of gods, an age of heroes, and an age of men, which he linked to the poetic tropes of metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and irony. A "barbarism of reflection" leads to collapse and a return (ricorso) to the start of the cycle.

**Historical materialism (Marx and Engels)**
In The German Ideology, Marx and Engels developed the materialist conception of history, which explains historical change by successive economic stages defined by their "modes of production." The Communist Manifesto opens by declaring that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

**Walter Benjamin, "Theses on the Philosophy of History"**
Benjamin's 1940 essay, also called "On the Concept of History," opens by comparing historical materialism to a chess-playing automaton like the Mechanical Turk, secretly operated by a hunchbacked dwarf representing theology. Its ninth thesis describes the "angel of history," based on Paul Klee's Angelus Novus, who sees the past as a single catastrophe piling wreckage upon wreckage.

**Hayden White, Metahistory**
White's 1973 book analyzes 19th-century historical writing with the tools of literary criticism. He argues that historians shape their narratives through modes of "emplotment" (romance, tragedy, comedy, satire), argument, and ideological implication, grounded in the four master tropes.

**Leopold von Ranke**
A 19th-century German historian who founded modern source-based historiography. He insisted that historians show the past "as it actually was" (wie es eigentlich gewesen) instead of passing moral judgment on it, an approach often called historical positivism.

**Michel Foucault, History of Madness and The Archaeology of Knowledge**
Foucault's History of Madness traces how Western society defined and confined the mad. In The Archaeology of Knowledge, he argued that the apparent continuities in the history of ideas break down into discontinuities on closer inspection.

**Alexandre Kojève**
A Russian-French philosopher whose 1930s Paris lectures on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit popularized the idea of an "end of history." His reading strongly influenced Fukuyama.

**George Santayana: "doomed to repeat it"**
In The Life of Reason, Santayana wrote that "those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." The line is often paraphrased in terms of being doomed to repeat history.

**E.H. Carr, What Is History?**
Carr's 1961 lectures argued that historical "facts" are selected and interpreted by the historian. He stressed the selectivity and subjectivity involved in writing history.

**Annales school and cliometrics**
The French Annales school, founded by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre and later led by Fernand Braudel, emphasized the longue durée, the long-term social, economic, and geographic structures of history. Cliometrics is the application of economic and statistical methods to history. The American Historical Review (AHR), a leading journal in the field, is based at Indiana University Bloomington.

**Bossuet, Discourse on Universal History**
Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, a 17th-century French bishop, wrote this 1681 work, which presents world history as unfolding under divine providence. It is an early example of the philosophy of history.
